title: Reform UK's £72 Million Windfall: Two Crypto Donors, One Record, Many Questions
summary:
In just two days, Reform UK received £72 million in donations — more than the total received by all UK political parties last year, which was just over £69 million. The staggering sum has triggered scrutiny, calls for donation caps, and a police investigation.

On Friday, cryptocurrency billionaire Ben Delo gave £36 million, the largest donation ever to a UK political party. On Saturday, Thailand-based crypto investor Christopher Harborne matched it. Harborne wrote in The Telegraph that his "competitive spirit" inspired him to equal Delo's gift, adding he expected "nothing personally" in return. Reform said the money would fund "the brightest and best minds" and up to 400 campaign managers in target constituencies. Leader Nigel Farage said the party could now "fight and win the next general election on a level playing field."

But the windfall raises questions. The government is seeking to cap donations from British expats, and rival parties want limits on individual donations. Police are investigating donations from Fiona Cottrell — mother of a longtime Farage ally — and a company controlled by Reform's Richard Tice. A Channel 4 News broadcast also showed two senior Reform aides appearing to suggest a way around electoral law on foreign donations. The party denies wrongdoing.

Harborne has already given millions to Reform and Farage. Farage is under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner over whether he should have declared a £5 million cash gift from Harborne before the 2024 election. Farage argues the gift was "purely private" and unrelated to his political role.

Harborne described Reform as a "start-up party" that lacks "hundreds of years of patronage" and needs more than membership fees to be ready for government.
why_it_matters: This story is really about political money: the rules deciding who may fund a party determine whose interests get heard at election time. If a couple of billionaires can bankroll an entire national campaign in two days, questions about influence, transparency and fairness move from the margins to the centre of British politics.

background_read: British election law is strict about where party money may come from: parties can only accept donations above a small threshold from 'permissible donors' — people on the UK electoral register, UK-registered companies and trade unions — and foreign donations are banned. The Electoral Commission, an independent regulator, publishes donations and can fine parties that break the rules.

Reform UK grew out of the Brexit Party, which Nigel Farage (the campaigner who pushed hardest for Britain to leave the European Union before the 2016 referendum) founded in 2018 and which was renamed Reform UK in 2021. The party won several seats at the 2024 general election, and Farage became an MP.

Ben Delo is a British-born crypto billionaire who co-founded the exchange BitMEX. Christopher Harborne is a British businessman based in Thailand who has already given millions to Reform UK and to Farage personally. Channel 4 News is the flagship news programme of a British public-service broadcaster.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — Reform UK and its supporters
perspectives.description: Reform argues it is a 'start-up party' that lacks the 'hundreds of years of patronage' older parties enjoy, so large donations simply let it compete on a 'level playing field'. Supporters say the money will pay for professional campaign staff and grassroots organising that membership fees alone could never fund.

Opponents warn that allowing individual mega-donations turns elections into auctions, and note that both gifts came from cryptocurrency fortunes rather than from any broad base of supporters. The police investigation, the Channel 4 News footage and the undeclared £5m gift all feed the argument that the rules are too weak.

Britain caps what parties may spend but not how much an individual may give, and regulators rely on disclosure rather than limits. The proposed cap on donations from British expats shows how a globalised, crypto-rich donor class is stretching a system designed for a very different era.

Several decisions will now set the boundaries for the next general election: whether Parliament caps individual donations, how the parliamentary standards commissioner rules on Farage's £5m gift, and what the police investigation concludes. Together they could reshape how every UK party is funded.
